text: The Tuareg are an Amazigh people of the Sahara desert and the Sahel.
Their founding queen Tin Hinan is believed to have lived over 1,500 years ago, and lies buried in the Hoggar Mountains.
src: The Tuareg are an Amazigh people of the Sahara and the Sahel
whose founding queen, Tin Hinan, is believed to have lived in the 4th or 5th century / her tomb stands at Abalessa in the Hoggar

text: They call themselves Imuhagh, and also Kel Tagelmust, which means “veiled people”.
Tuareg men, not women, traditionally cover their faces with an indigo veil, the tagelmust, once they grow up.
src: They call themselves Imuhagh or Imushagh / Kel Tagelmust, “veiled people”
Among the Tuareg it is the men, not the women, who traditionally veil their faces: a man takes on the tagelmust when he reaches maturity / the tagelmust, the indigo veil worn by men

text: They live from their herds and from trade, and for centuries their camel caravans carried salt across the Sahara.
Their society was ranked, from nobles at the top down to enslaved people at the bottom.
src: The Tuareg are a pastoral people, living from livestock, trade and farming / organised caravans across the Sahara, first with oxen and horses, later with camels, carrying salt
ranked into nobles, vassals, clerics, artisans and enslaved people / At the bottom were the enslaved, the ikelan

text: Most Tuareg are Muslims, and Tuareg clerics helped carry Islam across the Sahel.
Timbuktu, a city famed for its scholars, grew rich under the protection of the Tuareg.
src: they embraced the Maliki school of Sunni Islam, which most follow today / The clerical caste of the Ineslemen spread the faith across North Africa and the Sahel
Timbuktu, a centre famed for its scholars / flourished under a Tuareg confederation’s protection

text: The Tuareg fought hard against the French, who conquered their lands between 1881 and 1920.
In the 1960s their homeland was split among five new countries, and many Tuareg have since risen up for it.
src: The Tuareg resisted French conquest from 1881 to 1920
after independence their homeland was divided among five states / they have risen repeatedly for their homeland

text: Today more than a million Tuareg live in the Sahara and the Sahel, many of them in Niger.
Their smiths make silver jewellery such as the Agadez Cross, and festivals keep their music and dance alive.
src: an estimated 1.2 to 3 million people, about 2 million of them in Niger
Smiths of the inadan castes make jewellery of silver / the tanaghilt or Agadez Cross / Festivals such as the Festival in the Desert near Timbuktu gather Tuareg music and dance
